Handling & Authenticity
How to handle precious metals to preserve their value and verify authenticity using visual, physical, and professional methods.
Handling and Authenticity Verification
Proper handling preserves the condition (and resale value) of your precious metals. Authenticity verification protects you from counterfeits. Both are skills every investor should develop before accumulating any significant position.
Proper Handling Techniques
How you touch and store your metal directly affects its long-term value, especially for graded coins where surface marks can drop a grade and shave hundreds of dollars off price.
General Handling Rules
Clean hands:
Wash thoroughly before any session; skin oils etch surfaces over time.
Gloves:
Use lint-free cotton or nitrile.
Workspace:
Lay down velvet, felt, or a soft jeweler’s pad.
Grip:
Hold coins by the edges, bars by the corners. Never touch fields or devices.
Work over softness:
Drops onto hard surfaces dent edges and ruin proof finishes.
Metal-Specific Notes
Gold
is soft and scratches easily. Keep pieces in individual capsules or sleeves and avoid contact with dissimilar metals.
Silver
tarnishes when exposed to sulfur. Store in airtight containers with anti-tarnish strips, and avoid rubber bands, cardboard, and most papers, all of which off-gas sulfur compounds.
Platinum and palladium
are more durable than gold but can still develop patina. Store separately and keep storage clean and dry.
Storage Environment
Stable conditions matter more than fancy materials.
Humidity:
Target 30 to 50 percent relative humidity. Use silica gel packs in sealed containers.
Temperature:
Avoid swings; basements that flood with summer humidity are the worst offenders.
Air quality:
Keep metal away from cleaning chemicals, paints, and pool supplies.
Light:
Dark storage prevents toning on sensitive proof surfaces.
Safe storage materials include Mylar flips, archival plastic, Air-Tite capsules, and acid-free paper.
Avoid PVC plastics
(the green slime that develops on PVC-flipped coins is irreversible damage), rubber, newsprint, and untreated cardboard.
Authenticity Verification
Counterfeit precious metals are a real and growing problem, especially for popular sovereign coins and standard kilo and 10 oz bars. A layered approach works best: visual first, then physical tests, then electronics or professionals for high-value pieces.
Visual Inspection
Start with your eyes and a 10x loupe.
Color and luster:
Genuine gold and silver have characteristic reflectance. Plated fakes often look slightly off in tone or too “yellow.”
Edges:
Look for seams or tooling marks that suggest a filled or cast piece.
Markings:
Verify purity stamps, mint marks, fonts, and serial numbers against published references.
Wear patterns:
Genuine circulated coins wear evenly on high points. Cast copies often wear strangely or show casting bubbles.
Red flags include odd discoloration, pitted or rough fields, mismatched fonts, missing security features (micro-engraving, radial lines, latent images on modern sovereigns), and inconsistent strike depth.
Physical Tests
Magnet test.
Precious metals are not magnetic. A strong neodymium magnet will pull on iron- or nickel-cored fakes. A negative result does not prove authenticity (tungsten and lead are also non-magnetic), but a positive result is a near-certain fail.
Weight and dimension test.
Every sovereign coin and major bar has published weight, diameter, and thickness specs. Use a scale with at least 0.01 gram accuracy and calipers for diameter and thickness. Tungsten-filled gold bars can pass weight checks but usually fail on thickness because tungsten and gold have nearly identical density but slightly different volumes when machined.
Ping (sound) test.
Balance a coin on your fingertip and tap it with another coin. Silver produces a clear, sustained high-pitched ring; gold rings duller and shorter; base-metal fakes thud. Works best on coins, less reliable on bars.
Ice test (silver).
Silver has the highest thermal conductivity of any metal. An ice cube placed on a genuine silver bar melts noticeably faster than on any plated imitation.
Electronic and Advanced Testing
For larger purchases, electronic testers are worth the investment.
Sigma Metalytics Precious Metal Verifier:
Non-destructive electromagnetic test that reads the conductivity signature of the entire piece, including through plastic capsules. Catches tungsten-filled bars that fool every other simple test.
XRF analyzers:
X-ray fluorescence reads surface composition precisely. Useful for jewelry and odd-shape pieces, but only reads the top few microns, so it can be fooled by thick plating.
Ultrasonic thickness gauges:
Detect internal voids and inclusions in bars.
Acid tests still exist but mark the surface and are inappropriate for collectible or investment-grade pieces.
💡
When in doubt, don't buy
It is always better to miss a deal than to take home a counterfeit. If a price is well below the going market and the seller is unfamiliar, walk away. Stick to established dealers and use third-party grading for any significant rare coin.
Professional Authentication
For high-value or rare pieces, third-party grading services provide guaranteed authenticity, a condition grade, tamper-evident encapsulation, and insurance-friendly documentation. The major services are
PCGS
(Professional Coin Grading Service),
NGC
(Numismatic Guaranty Corporation),
ANACS
, and
ICG
. PCGS and NGC dominate the secondary market and their slabs typically command the strongest resale premium.
Send pieces in for grading when value justifies the fee, when authenticity is unclear, for estate or inherited holdings, and for anything destined for insurance scheduling.
Common Counterfeit Types
Plated:
Base metal with a thin precious metal coating. Easy to detect by weight, magnet, and ping.
Filled or clad:
A cheap core (often copper or tungsten) wrapped in genuine metal. Catches the casual buyer; defeated by Sigma testing or precise dimensions.
Cast copies:
Replicas molded from a real piece. Often show casting porosity and soft details.
Altered dates:
Common-date coins re-engraved to mimic rare dates. A grading service catches these immediately.
The most sophisticated fakes today are tungsten-filled gold bars in the kilo and 400 oz sizes, and very high-quality die-struck counterfeits of popular sovereign coins coming out of overseas workshops.
Documentation and Record Keeping
Keep purchase receipts, certificates of authenticity, photos of each piece, recorded weights, and any test results. A simple spreadsheet inventory with cloud backup is enough for most collectors and is invaluable for insurance claims and eventual sale or estate settlement.
Cleaning
The default answer is: don’t.
Never clean a collectible coin
— it destroys numismatic value, often irreversibly. Toning and natural patina are often desirable. For generic bullion bars or coins with visible grime, warm water and mild dish soap with a soft cloth is the most aggressive cleaning that is ever appropriate. Skip abrasives, polishes, and dips entirely unless you have consulted a professional.
Proper handling and authenticity verification are foundational skills. Build the habits early, invest in a decent scale and a magnet, and consider a Sigma tester once your holdings warrant it.
